A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiSeCo work despite the title change. The corresponding methods, equations, empirical figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original probing and toxicity/sentiment steering experiments on three language models, including probe-training sensitivity, already-safe generations, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v4 reports original results for the retained tasks and adds English–Spanish steering, out-of-distribution evaluations, and layer ablations.

M1.justification: v4 broadens the stated probe-training objective in Eq. 6 from binary cross-entropy to a user-defined loss, explicitly including mean-squared error. The closed-form minimum-norm controller is retained, and the experiments still specify cross-entropy training; this is a limited extension of the formulation.

E1.justification: v4 adds English–Spanish language steering using FLORES-Plus and tests transfer to Poetry Foundation poems, EuroParl proceedings, and CodeAlpaca snippets. These introduce a new attribute task, languages, and input domains beyond the retained toxicity and sentiment coverage.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparisons retain no-control, instruction-tuned prompting, ActAdd, and Linear AcT, also applying this set to language steering. However, the reported parameter-sweep comparison in Figure 6 removes the no-control reference shown in v2, although it remains in other figures.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates 1,000 sampled prompts per task. v4 filters toxicity/sentiment prompts to exclude undesirable prompt content and balances them by uncontrolled continuation outcomes, yielding 500 sentiment prompts and 186/160/180 toxicity prompts for Llama/Gemma/Mistral. The selected LiSeCo bounds change from [0, 0.01] to [0, 0.005]. New protocols include 200 balanced language prompts and 100 sequences per out-of-distribution dataset.

E4.justification: Appendix M adds a layer ablation testing single versus multiple interventions and early versus later layers. Section 6.4 and Appendix N add distribution-shift tests and failure examples, including delayed language switching and incorrect Romance-language outputs. The probe sample-size stress test and already-safe-generation analysis were already present in v2.

E5.justification: Both versions report probe accuracy across five random seeds with one standard deviation, generation comparison ellipses with one standard deviation, and generation fractions with one standard error. Additional uncertainty-bearing results in v4 do not establish a new reporting practice, increased run count, or new statistical test.

E6.justification: Figures 5, 6, K.1, and L.2 revise toxicity/sentiment output results under changed evaluation conditions, so these are not same-setting performance gains. v4 adds language, transfer, and layer-ablation results; Table 2 reports Gemma's mean Spanish probability as 0.913 in-distribution and 0.287 on code. The relocated qualitative example table also removes the LiSeCo 0.25 row.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 generalizes the loss formulation and removes v2's incorrect assertion that matching soft targets makes cross-entropy zero. Appendices D/E replace the two-column weight-difference expressions with W-based expressions. The principal controller theorem, Lemma C.1, and Appendix F propositions remain substantially unchanged; the revision does not add a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the empirical contribution to English–Spanish steering. v4 more explicitly presents activation control as a step toward the still-open problem of behavioral control. The central claims of constrained activation control, interpretable steering, and inexpensive closed-form intervention are retained.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that continuous training-score coverage explains better sentiment steerability than toxicity. v4 revises this explanation because binary-labeled language steering performs best. It also adds substantive limitations concerning model-dependent transfer, linear decodability, binary attributes, and delayed intervention on already-undesirable prompts, positioning LiSeCo primarily as preemptive steering.

D1.justification: v2 promises code and data release upon acceptance; v4 provides a specific repository as their access location. Appendix B adds precise classifier and new dataset identifiers, while Appendices I/J document the Spanish instruction and hello/hola ActAdd prompts. Existing hardware, probe hyperparameters, and runtime estimates are retained. Repository availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations including Im and Li on steering evaluation, Lad et al. on inference stages, Wolf et al. on alignment limitations, and Macocco et al. on effectiveness–fluency tradeoffs, alongside new dataset/scorer references. The central positioning against existing intervention families, AcT, and ReFT remains intact.

P1.justification: Substantial rewriting and reorganization include moving the contributions before Related Work, revising the problem and probe-training exposition, and restructuring experimental subheadings and discussion. The paper is retitled and adds explicit limitations, acknowledgments, and publication information.

P2.justification: Figures 3–6 and appendix plots expand to include language steering, with substantial changes to panel arrangements, axes, and captions. v4 adds transfer, layer-ablation, and qualitative-example tables; v2 Table M.1 becomes a condensed Table N.2. Figure 6 removes baseline bars while retaining caption references to them.

improvement.justification: The layer ablation and transfer tests strengthen scrutiny of intervention placement and applicability, while the language results motivate revision of v2's label-coverage explanation. Clearer practical limitations and reported code/data access also improve assessability. These gains are qualified by smaller, benign-prompt-only toxicity/sentiment evaluations and presentation inconsistencies, including Figure 5's language-axis labeling and Figure 6's references to removed baselines. Appendix D's inverse-function inconsistency also remains unresolved.
